Article Title: Taiwan detains communist party leader over alleged links to China ahead of local polls
Article Text:
File photo: Chairman of Taiwan People's Communist Party Lin Te-wang (center)

Prosecutors allege vote-buying and links to China

Lin had faced earlier charges over alleged Chinese links

Taiwan's local polls come amid tensions with Beijing

Authorities in Taiwan have detained the leader of the island's Taiwan People's Communist Party over allegations that he ran as a candidate for borough chief under the direction and sponsorship of China's Communist Party, local media reported on Sunday.Lin Te-wang, the party's chair, is also accused of directing another party member to contest for the post of chief in a separate borough, according to Taiwan's Central News Agency (CNA), which cited a statement by prosecutors.Taiwan is scheduled to hold elections for mayors and local area chiefs on November 28. While the contests largely focus on local livelihood issues, the results could indicate the popularity of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), led by President Lai Ching-te, ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Prosecutors alleged that Lin attempted to buy votes by repeatedly recruiting voters to travel to mainland China, where they were provided hospitality, CNA reported.The prosecutors said they had received intelligence about possible foreign interference in the elections and summoned 14 people and nine witnesses as part of the investigation.After questioning those involved, prosecutors suspected that Lin and the other party member had committed offences.They also expressed concerns that the two could flee or destroy evidence, prompting them to seek court orders for their detention and restrictions on visits.The courts approved the application to detain Lin. The other party member was released on bail of 50,000 Taiwan dollars (around $525), while the remaining people summoned were released during the investigation.Lin's party has limited influence on the democratic island, but this is not the first time he has faced legal action over alleged links with Beijing.Lin and another party leader had previously faced charges of Chinese infiltration and attempting to influence elections. However, both were found not guilty in 2025, the Taipei Times reported.The November 28 elections are being held against the backdrop of longstanding tensions between Taiwan and China.Beijing considers Taiwan a breakaway province and has not ruled out using force to bring the island under its control.Allegations of Chinese interference have frequently surfaced during Taiwanese elections.China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949, when the Chinese Communist Party came to power in Beijing following a civil war.Forces belonging to the defeated Nationalist Party fled to Taiwan, which later transitioned from martial law to a multiparty democracy.
Article Summary: Prosecutors allege vote-buying and links to China. Lin Te-wang, the party's chair, is also accused of directing another party member to contest for the post of chief in a separate borough. Lin had faced earlier charges over alleged Chinese links.

Article Title: The great White mix-up: Did Trump offer White House job to the wrong Dana White?
Article Text:
The wrong Dana? Trump offers UFC chief White House job, internet spots possible mix-up

Internet spots a possible Dana White mix-up

Did US President Donald Trump mistake UFC boss Dana White for another Dana White while offering the White House press secretary's job? That is the question doing the rounds online after an apparent name mix-up triggered a wave of jokes, speculation and confusion.Trump on Saturday announced that he had offered the high-profile White House role to Dana White, president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) and one of his longtime allies.However, the announcement quickly became a talking point after social media users suggested the president may have confused him with Dana W White, a former Assistant to the secretary of defense for public affairs.The UFC chief eventually turned down the offer, CNN reported."I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States. Dana, please take the job!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.White appeared to initially play along with the announcement, sharing an Instagram story featuring himself against a White House backdrop, with the US flag in the background and the caption, "On to the next chapter."He also reposted a screenshot of Trump's announcement, further fuelling speculation about whether the offer was genuine.The announcement soon attracted a different kind of attention, with users speculating that Trump may have intended to appoint Dana W White, a former Pentagon public affairs official, rather than the UFC executive.Spencer T Hakimian, founder of New York-based hedge fund Tolou Capital Management, shared a video suggesting that the president may have confused the two."I guarantee you 100%, somebody recommended her to Trump and he mistook her for the UFC's Dana White and now we all are in this mess," he joked.Another US-based user wrote, "Oh my god someone told Trump to pick DoD Spox and ex-House GOP flak Dana White as Press Secretary and he thought they meant Dana White the CEO of UFC."A third post similarly claimed that Dana W White, who had handled public affairs for the defence secretary, was reportedly recommended for the position."Apparently 'Dana W. White' who ran public affairs for Sec Def was recommended on a short list for Trump to put as Press Secretary.Trump has instead announced 'Dana White' of the UFC as Press Secretary with our Dana having any idea," the user wrote.The online chatter, however, centred on speculation about a possible mix-up, rather than any confirmed explanation for Trump's announcement.
Article Summary: Internet spots possible Dana White mix-up as US President Donald Trump offers UFC boss White House job. Social media users suggest the president may have confused him with Dana W White, a former Assistant to the secretary of defense for public affairs. The UFC chief eventually turned down the offer, CNN reported.

Article Title: 'No business being in NATO': Presidential hopeful Melenchon pitches radical new course for France
Article Text:
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of French far-left opposition party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed - LFI) and candidate for the 2027 French presidential election, delivers a speech during a political rally to present LFI's government program for the presidential election

Economic and welfare promises

Nuclear energy and EU policy

Melenchon's electoral prospects

French presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon on Saturday pledged an economic stimulus programme, including price controls, higher minimum wages and increased taxes on the wealthy, while renewing his call for France to withdraw from NATO. The 75-year-old leader of the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party unveiled his 2027 presidential programme at a rally in Le Bourget, near Paris, outlining plans to reverse President Emmanuel Macron's economic policies."We are going to do exactly the opposite — that is to say, a policy of stimulus," Melenchon told supporters at the rally, which drew around 17,000 people, according to his campaign director Manuel Bompard.He said the proposed stimulus would focus on boosting consumer spending and directing existing savings towards social and environmental needs."We have no business being in NATO, nor in American wars," Melenchon said, reiterating his opposition to France's membership of the military alliance. His programme calls for a gradual withdrawal, beginning with an exit from NATO's integrated military command. He also proposed building "a global front of non-aligned countries".Melenchon's programme, titled "L'Avenir en commun" (A Shared Future), promises measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis. These include freezing prices, raising the minimum wage and linking wages to inflation.The party wants to increase the net monthly minimum wage to 1,700 euros from around 1,480 euros. It has also proposed capping prices of essential food items, scrapping the flat tax on capital income and increasing taxes on the wealthiest households.The manifesto also promises to reverse Macron's pension reform, which gradually increased the minimum retirement age from 62 to 64 to strengthen public finances. Melenchon wants to restore retirement at 60 for people who have contributed to the pension system for 40 years.On energy, LFI has reiterated its support for gradually phasing out nuclear power and moving towards an electricity system powered entirely by renewable sources.The programme proposes scrapping the planned EPR2 nuclear reactor programme and ruling out extensions to the operating lives of nuclear plants beyond 60 years.It also criticises Germany's influence over European Union economic policy. The manifesto describes Berlin as the bloc's leading defender of "ordoliberalism", an economic philosophy that emphasises strict budget rules, price stability and independent monetary policy.Melenchon is seen as the strongest contender on the French left ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Recent opinion polls suggest he could reach the second round in April next year against far-right leader Marine Le Pen.However, the same polls indicate that he could lose to Le Pen in the runoff.The latest manifesto is the fifth edition of LFI's programme. It largely retains policies that have formed the basis of Melenchon's previous presidential campaigns.
Article Summary: French presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon pledges an economic stimulus programme. The 75-year-old leader of the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party unveiled his 2027 presidential programme at a rally in Le Bourget, near Paris. His programme calls for a gradual withdrawal from NATO's integrated military command.

Article Title: A New York bank filed to foreclose on a married couple's home, missed a 2017 court deadline and let its case be dismissed in 2019; after waiting more than six years to revive the case, it lost another
Article Text:
A New York court rejected the bank's bid to reopen a foreclosure case dismissed in 2019 after a six-year delay. (AI image)

Bank could not explain why it missed deadlines

Court rejects bank's other arguments

A New York bank has failed in its attempt to restart a home foreclosure case after allowing it to remain inactive for more than six years. The bank had started legal proceedings against a married couple over their home in Sullivan County, New York, but missed a deadline set by the court in 2017. The case was eventually dismissed in 2019.Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas had approached the court after an alleged default on a loan taken by David A. Leis. The loan was secured by a mortgage on a residential property signed by Leis and his wife, Marie Leis.According to the ruling , as part of the foreclosure proceedings, the court directed the bank in March 2017 to file a required application by December 31 that year. It also warned the bank that the case could be removed from the court calendar if it missed the deadline. If the bank did not take steps to bring the case back within a year, it could be dismissed.The bank failed to submit the application on time. In January 2018, the court informed it that the case had been removed from the calendar. The bank then missed another opportunity to act. It did not ask the court to restart the case within the next year.As a result, the court dismissed the foreclosure case on January 7, 2019. The dismissal was without prejudice, meaning the court did not rule on the merits of the bank's foreclosure claim.However, the bank did not approach the court again until February 2025. It asked for the dismissal to be cancelled and the case to be restored to the active list. The court rejected the request in April 2025, prompting the bank to appeal.On Thursday, the New York Supreme Court's Appellate Division, Third Department, upheld that decision. The judges said the bank had not given a convincing explanation for failing to meet the deadline or for waiting more than six years to challenge the dismissal.The appellate court noted that the bank had been clearly warned about what would happen if it failed to meet the December 2017 deadline. Despite this, it neither filed the required application nor asked the court for more time.The bank also failed to act after receiving the January 2018 notice that the case had been removed from the calendar. It then allowed the matter to remain inactive until February 2025 before asking the court to reopen it.The judges said the bank had not provided an affidavit from its lawyer or any other person with direct knowledge of the case. Such a statement could have explained why the deadline was missed, why the bank did not respond to the court's notice and why it took so long to seek the restoration of the case.The bank referred to earlier court decisions in which mistakes made by lawyers or their offices had been accepted as reasons for missing deadlines. However, the judges said the bank had not identified any such mistake.It did not point to a specific error in recording the deadline, a communication problem within the law office or any other incident that could explain its failure to act. It also gave no reason for waiting more than six years to challenge the dismissal.The bank also argued that the couple had not filed a notice of entry for the 2019 dismissal order. It suggested that this was relevant to the delay in seeking to reopen the case.The appellate court disagreed. It said the notice of entry affected the time available to file a request to cancel the dismissal. However, it did not explain why the bank had failed to follow the court's earlier directions or provide a reasonable reason for its prolonged inaction.The judges said the lower court was justified in rejecting the bank's request because it had failed to explain its conduct.They also said there was no need to examine whether the bank had a valid foreclosure claim. Before considering that question, the bank first had to explain why it had missed the deadlines. Since it failed to do so, the court did not need to examine the strength of its original case.The bank further argued that the lower court should have used its authority to reopen the matter in the interest of justice. The appellate judges examined this argument along with its other remaining claims but found them unconvincing.

Article Title: Researchers surveyed 1,500 km of ancient Arabian desert and checked 125 sites, finding evidence of lakes at 55 but no early human tools; a new study suggests missing toolmaking stone mattered as much
Article Text:
Scientists have made new discoveries about the Arabian peninsula.

What was Green Arabia ?

The missing ingredient: stone

Water and stone: A combination for survival

What does this change about human migration ?

Simple fifth-grade science would have us believe that we need just three things to survive: air, water and food. So, when scientists discovered evidence of freshwater lakes across the interiors of the Arabian Peninsula, they expected to find traces of large prehistoric human settlements. Surprisingly, most archaeological evidence of human occupation was found around the desert's outskirts, rather than its water-rich interior. What was keeping humans away? new study published in Nature on 28 October 2026 offers an interesting explanation. Researchers suggest that early humans did not simply settle wherever they found freshwater. They also needed access to particular types of stone to make tools, which were essential to their everyday survival.You would be surprised to know that the dry, arid sea of sand that the Arabian Peninsula is today was, at multiple points throughout history, considerably greener. This is what scientists refer to as ‘Green Arabia’.Over the past eight million years, large parts of the peninsula have experienced repeated periods of wetter weather, supporting lakes, rivers, grasslands and vegetation. However, Green Arabia was not one continuous period of greenness.These humid phases were separated by dry intervals, and the entire peninsula was not necessarily green at the same time.Scientists have established this through several forms of geological evidence. Ancient lake deposits, or palaeolakes, contain layers of sediments, minerals, shells and other biological remains that indicate the presence of freshwater. Fossils of animals such as hippopotamuses and crocodiles, which depend on aquatic environments, also suggest that parts of Arabia once supported very different ecosystems. Researchers have even studied mineral formations called speleothems, which develop when mineral-rich water drips through limestone caves, leaving behind layers of calcium carbonate.However, despite the presence of ancient lakes in the interior, known evidence of prehistoric human occupation was concentrated around the edges of the Arabian desert. If freshwater was available, why were humans not settling further inside?To investigate this, an international team of researchers conducted a large archaeological and geological survey across the Rub' al Khali, also known as the Empty Quarter. It is the world's largest continuous sand sea, stretching across parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE and Yemen.Between 15 November and 20 December 2023, the team travelled approximately 1,500 kilometres across the desert over 35 days. They examined 125 locations, looking for evidence of ancient lakes, freshwater, stone suitable for making prehistoric tools and fragments of materials that could indicate human activity.At 55 of the 125 locations, they discovered evidence of ancient lakes. These included freshwater mollusc shells, ostrich eggshell fragments and sediment deposits left behind by ancient water bodies.However, there was something missing. Despite finding evidence of freshwater, researchers found no stone tools, no traces of human toolmaking and no suitable stone that early humans could have used to manufacture tools along the surveyed interior route.This is because early humans depended heavily on stone tools for everyday survival. They used them to cut meat, process plants, scrape animal hides and prepare other materials. But not every rock is suitable for making a tool. They needed what archaeologists call knappable stone, a material that could be chipped and shaped into sharp edges without breaking unpredictably.The researchers found that the central Arabian basin largely lacked these suitable rocks. More than 95% of the ground surface was visible during their survey, making it reasonably possible to spot archaeological remains if they were present.The researchers did not stop at their desert expedition. They also created geographical models to understand how the availability of water and stone influenced prehistoric human settlements across the Arabian Peninsula.They compared 363 known prehistoric archaeological sites with the availability of freshwater and suitable stone. Their findings revealed that approximately 57% of the peninsula's water-accessible terrain sits on geological formations that lack suitable stone for making tools.Thus, having freshwater did not necessarily make a location suitable for sustained human settlement.When researchers included the availability of stone in their models, their predictions of where early humans actually settled became more accurate. Humans were more likely to establish themselves in places where both essential resources existed together.The researchers describe this landscape as a lithic archipelago. Think of an archipelago as a collection of islands. Here, the islands were pockets of land where freshwater and suitable rocks were both available. These could support human populations, while the vast stretches between them were considerably less suitable.Until now, researchers studying prehistoric human migration have largely relied on climate records, rainfall patterns and evidence of ancient lakes to predict where humans could have lived. This study suggests that geology deserves just as much attention.It also raises an interesting possibility: the absence of archaeological evidence in certain regions does not necessarily mean humans never explored them. They may have encountered landscapes that had water but lacked the materials they needed to maintain their everyday tools.Of course, the researchers have not proved that nobody ever entered the interior of the Rub' al Khali. Their survey found no archaeologically visible evidence of occupation along the investigated route, and their findings suggest that sustained settlements were more likely where water and suitable stone occurred together.Human migration is influenced by more than favourable weather and the availability of food and water. Sometimes, the difference between a place humans could visit and a place they could actually settle in came down to the rocks beneath their feet.
Article Summary: Scientists have made new discoveries about the Arabian peninsula. Despite finding evidence of freshwater, researchers found no stone tools, no traces of human toolmaking and no suitable stone that early humans could have used to manufacture tools. This is because early humans depended heavily on stone tools for everyday survival. But not every rock is suitable for making a tool.

Article Title: Hair and nail tests on eight frozen Inca mummies sacrificed on Andean volcanoes show every one had chewed coca leaves, four had drunk alcohol, and the famous Juanita mummy had taken a plant used in ay
Article Text:
What were the rituals of the Incan empire? Image credits: WikiMedia Commons

What was the Capacocha?

capacocha

What the new study found

Male figurines from Llullaillaco and Ampato with coca pulp inside cheeks Image Credits: J. Reinhard

Juanita and the Ayahuasca clue

Juanita, one of the sacrificed Inca mummiesImage Credits: Dr. Dagmara Socha

Banisteriopsis

Banisteriopsis

Not one ritual, but many

A story preserved in hair

High in the Andes, where the air is thin and the mountains seem closer to the sky than to the earth, archaeologists have uncovered a haunting glimpse into one of the Inca Empire’s most sacred ceremonies. Eight frozen mummies of children and young people who were sacrificed more than 500 years ago have now told researchers what they consumed in the days and months before their deaths. Their hair and nails preserved the evidence: coca leaves in every case, alcohol in four, and, in one famous girl known as Juanita, a compound linked to ayahuasca. The findings do not simply confirm that the Inca used psychoactive plant; but also reveal how priests prepared each child for a ritual that was meant to connect the living world with the gods.The ritual was called the, one of the most important religious ceremonies in the Inca Empire. Children and young women were selected and taken to high mountain shrines, where they were sacrificed as offerings to powerful deities. In Inca belief, these victims became sacred messengers, travelling from the human world into the divine realm.The ceremonies were often carried out during moments of crisis.Drought, famine, disease, political unrest, or the fear that the natural order had been disturbed could prompt the state to seek the favour of mountain gods. These deities were believed to control weather, water, fertility and harvests: forces on which Andean communities depended for survival.But the capacocha was an act of desperation, and at the same time, deeply political. By choosing children from different regions and bringing them into an imperial religious ceremony, the Inca state reinforced its authority and connected local communities to the empire’s central power. For the families involved, selection could bring prestige, even as it meant losing a child.The children were treated with extraordinary care before the final ritual. Historical accounts describe long journeys, ceremonial meals, fine clothing and sacred objects. Yet until recently, scientists knew relatively little about what substances the victims were given, or how their preparation differed from one mountain shrine to another.A research team led by Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw analysed hair and nail samples from 8 frozen Inca mummies found on mountains in Peru and Argentina. The children were between 6-14 years old when they died, roughly 5 centuries ago. The study, published in Antiquity , used modern toxicological methods capable of detecting even tiny traces of substances preserved in keratin, the protein that makes up hair and nails.Cocaine, the chemical marker left behind after chewing coca leaves, was found in all eight mummies. This confirms that every child chewed coca before death. Coca held a sacred place in the Inca religion, but it also had a practical purpose. It could reduce hunger, ease fatigue and help the body cope with the punishing altitude of the Andes.Four of the mummies showed evidence of alcohol consumption. Researchers believe this was likely chicha, a fermented maize beer. Spanish-era accounts suggest that children were given chicha in the final stages of the ritual to calm them, dull their senses and make the experience less frightening.In two mummies, including one from Llullaillaco, researchers also detected cocaethylene, a compound the body produces when cocaine and alcohol are consumed together. That detail suggests that coca and chicha were used in combination, perhaps deliberately, during the final approach to sacrifice.The most unexpected discovery involved Juanita, also known as the Lady of Ampato. Her mummy was found on Ampato, a Peruvian volcano, in 1995, and she remains one of the most famous Inca sacrificial victims ever discovered.In Juanita’s fingernails, scientists identified harmine, an alkaloid associated withplants, key ingredients in ayahuasca. No other mummy in the study showed traces of harmine. This suggests that Juanita was given a drink containing this plant, and that it had a particular meaning in the ceremonies connected with Ampato. Researchers believe harmine may have been used to lift her mood, reduce fear and alter her state of consciousness before death. Moreover, the presence of, grown in the Amazon rainforest, suggests long-distance trade networks.The capacocha was not a single fixed ceremony. The substances given to each child varied. Coca appears to have been common, but alcohol and harmine were not found in every case.This suggests that priests adapted the ritual to local traditions, sacred landscapes and the specific deities being honoured. A mountain God associated with water may have demanded a different offering than one linked to fertility or protection. In this sense, the capacocha was less a rigid imperial formula and more a flexible religious system shaped by place, belief and circumstance.The evidence also complicates easy assumptions. The substances may have helped calm the children, but they do not erase the violence of what happened to them. Researchers cannot reconstruct exactly how these young people felt. Being chosen for a prestigious ceremony did not mean the experience was not frightening or traumatic.The research is intimate, analysed through the hairs and nails of the Incan children. While it is unfair to judge the rituals of the past by modern standards, it is a look into the past rituals. It is important to understand these are not fictional stories; these are the stories of real people. Children who walked long distances, climbed freezing mountains and faced a fate decided by adults, priests and rulers.The new analysis does not solve every mystery. Some substances may never have entered hair or nails, and drugs given only in the final moments may leave no trace. But it brings us closer to understanding the capacocha.
Article Summary: Eight frozen mummies of children and young people who were sacrificed more than 500 years ago have now told researchers what they consumed. Their hair and nails preserved the evidence: coca leaves in every case, alcohol in four, and, in one famous girl known as Juanita, a compound linked to ayahuasca. The findings do not simply confirm that the Inca used psychoactive plant; but also reveal how priests prepared each child for a ritual.

Article Title: Midterm losses, no exits: Marco Rubio rules out quitting, Donald Trump backs Pete Hegseth
Article Text:
File photo - US President Donald Trump speaks during a media conference as Marco Rubio, right, and Pete Hegseth listen

Rubio backs JD Vance for 2028 presidential race

White House rejects reports of Rubio's possible exit

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections, saying that completing President Donald Trump's second term has “always been my plan”.In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign and declined to discuss his political ambitions.“Working for President Trump until the end of his term has always been my plan,” Rubio said, adding that he did not know where reports about his possible departure had originated.“I love the work I’m doing,” he said. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”Rubio, who also serves as Trump's national security adviser, refused to entertain questions about whether he was considering a presidential run in 2028.“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he told the newspaper in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”Rubio has previously indicated that he would support Vice President JD Vance if he decided to run for president in 2028.“JD is a very good friend of mine,” Rubio told NBC News in May. “If JD runs for president, I think he’d be a phenomenal candidate. I’ve said publicly, and I’ll say it again, I’ll be the first person to sign up and support him.”However, Vance's post-election assessment on Wednesday included criticism of the administration's approach to the Iran war, its policy on Israel and its messaging on the economy.The vice-president blamed the war with Iran for the Republicans' election setbacks and said voters had turned against the administration's position on Israel and its handling of economic concerns. Trump has closely aligned himself with Israel and dismissed concerns over affordability as a “hoax”.Asked whether he agreed with Vance's assessment, Rubio initially deflected, saying he was not “really involved in domestic politics”.However, Rubio acknowledged the political implications of the Iran war when he appeared alongside Trump at a rally in Kansas on Sunday. Trump praised the secretary of state and joked that he might have to fire him because he had become “too popular”.Explaining his presence at the rally, Rubio said he was travelling with the president as the designated national security official. He also acknowledged Trump's remarks that the war had been a factor in the election results.“Higher prices at the gas pump, I acknowledge, is not like the kind of thing you campaign on and brag about,” Rubio said.However, he defended Trump's decision to take action despite its potential political costs, saying the president “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for doing what he considered necessary.“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position following the Republican setbacks.White House spokesperson Beni Rae Harmony described the reports as a fabricated hoax circulated by anonymous sources, while assistant secretary of state for global public affairs Dylan Johnson called them baseless fake news.The speculation over a possible administration shake-up has also involved defence secretary Pete Hegseth , whose handling of the Iran war has drawn criticism following the election losses.The White House has denied reports that Hegseth and Rubio might leave their positions. Trump told ABC News that he had received calls about Hegseth but had “every intention” of keeping him. He later praised the defence secretary, saying he had “done a fantastic job”.However, Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he intends to move ahead with an effort to impeach Hegseth, with a resolution expected as early as next week. Hegseth has rejected the effort, describing it as a politically motivated attempt to undermine him.Separately, The Washington Post reported that Trump could be considering replacing General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command.Both have played significant roles in providing guidance on the Iran war.
Article Summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections. In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign. The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position.

Article Text:

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Nithya Raman's background

Indian origin winners from the US midterm elections

Nithya Raman stood before supporters at a downtown Los Angeles brewery in June, struggling to hold back tears. The early primary election returns had placed her third in the race for mayor, behind incumbent Karen Bass and reality tv personality Spencer Pratt, and it looked like the end of the road for her. She gave what was almost a concession speech. Her father Venkit Raman, an IITian, comforted campaign workers, telling them her full name Nithya Varsha means 'everlasting monsoon,' and her political life would be replenished soon.It came sooner than anyone expected because after all this is the la la land of Hollywood where plot twists are common. And appropriately too enough considering her husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a successful television writer and producer whose credits include 30 Rock and Modern Family. A batch of late ballots that came in took Raman past Pratt to second place, and because Bass did not get 50 per cent of the vote, there would be a run-off election in November. Even then, few gave the 45-year old political tyro, with only six years of experience on the City Council, any chance. Raman herself had once supported Bass, and the 73-year old party stalwart had the backing of the Democratic establishment, including endorsements from Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi and Governor Gavin Newsom.She had experience, name recognition, and the advantage of incumbency.What Bass could not quite escape was the perception that Los Angeles is broken and she did not have the toolkit to fix it. The devastating January 2025 Palisades wildfire, which killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes, became a defining political liability. Bass was abroad when the mishap occurred and her handling of the disaster and recovery became a persistent political liability. Raman’s campaign ignited. She offered herself as the candidate of change, promising better housing, improved public services and more accountable government. An urban planner by training, she could talk about the nuts and bolts of city administration rather than simply deliver ideological sermons. On Tuesday night, her persistence paid off, and although the race has not been officially called, she is ahead by 25,000 votes and looks likely to seal the deal. She invited supporters to join her in a dance on Wednesday, the tears in June now forgotten.Raman's victory is more than an extraordinary personal turnaround. It is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been steadily challenging the Democratic Party establishment. And for India, it provides an especially striking political subplot: New York and Los Angeles, America's two largest cities, will now be led by mayors of Indian origin, with Zohran Mamdani already in office in New York.What's even more striking: Long before Mamdani and Raman began making their mark in American municipal politics, several prominent Indian nationalists and intellectuals had encountered the country's radical political traditions first hand. Lala Lajpat Rai spent five years in the U.S between 1914 and 1919, establishing the India Home Rule League and publishing the journal Young India in New York. The radical humanist M.N. Roy arrived in the U.S in 1916 as a global itinerant, encountered American radicals and began studying socialism, subsequently moving to Mexico City, where he founded the Communist Party of Mexico in 1919. He later played a foundational role in establishing the Communist Party of India in 1920. B.R. Ambedkar, meanwhile, studied at Columbia University in NYC, encountering some of America's leading liberal and progressive intellectuals, including philosopher John Dewey. And Jayaprakash Narayan spent seven years in America (1922-1929), studying at Berkeley, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where he encountered Marxism and returned to India a committed socialist.All this was at a time socialism was enjoying considerable electoral popularity. In 1912, Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes, then about 6% of the national total. Socialists also held hundreds of municipal offices, including mayoralties. In fact, in the early 1950s Donald Trump’s father Fred Trump clashed with the folk singer Woody Guthrie, an avowed socialist, over racial segregation and housing discrimination in Brooklyn, causing him to write a song -- a scalding takedown of a predatory landlord -- titled “Old Man Trump" who stirred up racial hatred "in the bloodsport of the human heart. "Indeed, even in the modern era, the current upsurge of socialists did not emerge overnight. One of its earliest conspicuous faces was another Indian activist: Kshama Sawant, born in Pune and raised in Mumbai, who won a seat on Seattle's City Council in 2013. A former economics professor and member of Socialist Alternative rather than the DSA, Sawant became a prominent voice for a $15 minimum wage, rent control and taxing the wealthy. Her victory demonstrated that a politician openly identifying with socialism could win in an American city.Bernie Sanders subsequently took the argument national with his presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020 bringing democratic socialism into mainstream political conversation, particularly among younger Americans frustrated by inequality, expensive healthcare, housing costs and the influence of corporate money. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's (AOC’s) stunning 2018 primary victory over veteran Democrat Joe Crowley gave the movement another national face. The election of Mamdani as New York mayor in 2025 was an even bigger breakthrough. Mamdani defeated Democratic political heavyweight Andrew Cuomo by campaigning on affordable housing, free bus services, universal childcare and a city government that would work for ordinary people.The movement now has a growing presence in municipal government. Besides Mamdani in New York, democratic socialist or DSA-affiliated mayors include Katie Wilson in Seattle, Janeese Lewis George in Washington DC, Emma Mulvaney-Stanak in Burlington, Robert Cantelmo in Ithaca and Eduardo Martinez in Richmond, California. In the mid-terms, six DSA-endorsed candidates have won seats in the House of Representatives: Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York (both backed by Mamdani), Melat Kiros in Colorado, Angela Gonzales-Torres in California, Donavan McKinney in Michigan and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib also won re-election.The organisation's own election tracker reported victories across an even wider range of state and local contests, including in Florida, Maryland, Washington, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Vermont. The significance is not simply the number of elected socialists, but their willingness, like in the case of Raman v Bass, to challenge Democratic incumbents and party leadership rather than wait patiently for establishment approval.While their electoral success is undeniable, the jury is still out on their ability to translate ambitious promises of affordable housing, safer streets, better transport and sustainable municipal finances into reality. Governing New York or Seattle or LA is considerably more complicated than winning an election with a catchy slogan. Already, MAGA bros are cranking up right wing fearmongering with Conservative commentators Benny Johnson invoking scenarios of urban 'Armageddon' a favorite Trump theme.For now though the socialists are having their moment in the sun. The MAGA crowd is predicting an apocalypse, the billionaires are checking their property portfolios, and the Democratic establishment is wondering whether it should start taking out membership in the DSA. Raman and Mamdani now have the rather unenviable task of proving that running a city is not quite the same as running against one. In the process, America's urban political landscape is getting a makeover — and this time, the revolution has an Indian accent.
Article Summary: Nithya Raman and Zohran Mamdani are the new mayors of Los Angeles and New York City respectively. Raman's victory is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been challenging the Democratic Party establishment.

Article Title: A Scottish wildlife rescuer saved a starving badger cub trapped in a cattle trough, but officials denied his request to keep her; now he is fighting to retain the animal he says cannot survive in the
Article Text:
Rescued from a cattle trough in April, Harriet was nursed back to health by ecologist Graeme Wilson.

From a desperate rescue to an unusual bond

Why the ecologist wants to keep Harriet

Wildlife experts raise concerns

Harriet's future remains uncertain

Images Courtesy: istock and BBC

A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human intervention. When Scottish ecologist Graeme Wilson rescued a starving badger cub from a cattle trough, he expected to nurse her back to health. Instead, the experience left him convinced that returning her to the wild could put her life in danger. Now, he is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities.According to the BBC, Harriet was discovered in April trapped inside a cattle trough, around 100 metres from her sett in the Scottish Borders. Wilson was called to help the young animal and took responsibility for her recovery, gradually nursing her back to health.However, her behaviour soon raised concerns about whether she could survive independently. Given her bottle feeding response and familiarity with humans, Wilson suspected Harriet was hand-reared before her rescue.As reported by The Telegraph, Wilson believes the cub has become accustomed to humans to such an extent that releasing her into the countryside could expose her to serious risks. He fears she might approach people while out walking, potentially placing herself in a dangerous situation.Wilson operates GW Ecology, an independent wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service from his home in Denholm. Alongside caring for injured animals, his work involves ecological surveys to identify protected species at proposed development sites. He also organises bat walks, workshops and educational activities to encourage greater awareness of wildlife conservation.The ecologist applied to NatureScot for an educational licence that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet while helping the public understand badgers and the challenges involved in rehabilitating protected wildlife.However, the application was rejected. NatureScot suggested that Harriet should either be returned to the wild or transferred to a zoo. Wilson believes neither option would adequately address her circumstances. While a release could expose her to injury or death, he fears a conventional zoo environment would leave her isolated and distressed.The disagreement has brought wider questions about the responsibilities involved in wildlife rehabilitation into focus. The BBC reported that the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.Paul Reynolds, who chairs the organisation, has highlighted the importance of suitable facilities, species-specific care, veterinary supervision and an understanding of an animal's natural behaviour. The council also distinguishes responsible rehabilitation from keeping wild animals permanently in captivity for educational or personal purposes.According to The Telegraph, the organisation maintains that an animal becoming accustomed to human contact should not automatically be considered grounds for permanent captivity.NatureScot has indicated that discussions with Wilson and other relevant organisations are continuing in an effort to find a practical resolution. The authority has emphasised that Harriet's welfare remains central to its decision-making process. Police Scotland has also been made aware of the situation.Meanwhile, the Scottish SPCA advises people who encounter sick or injured badgers to contact its rescue officers rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves. Young cubs found away from their setts may need help, and frightened or injured badgers may attack.Wilson still wants a safe future for Harriet. Whether that means an exception to the usual rules or another arrangement, the case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.
Article Summary: Harriet the badger cub was rescued from a cattle trough in April. Ecologist Graeme Wilson nursed her back to health but is now fighting for permission to give her a permanent home. The British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.

Article Title: Massachusetts neighbours spent years complaining about sand, dust and noise from an adjoining mine; in August 2026, a jury awarded the couple $530,000 after finding the operators liable for property i
Article Text: A Massachusetts couple who spent years dealing with dust, noise and vibrations from a neighbouring sand mining operation have won $530,000 in damages after a jury found the operators liable for the impact on their property. The verdict, delivered on August 11, 2026, in Plymouth Superior Court, followed a lengthy legal battle involving complaints about airborne sand, heavy truck traffic and potential exposure to silica dust. Details of the case were reported by the Community Land & Water Coalition, with further coverage from the Plymouth Independent and legal publication Exlitem. Josephine and Keith Beadling brought the case against G. Lopes Construction Inc. and landowner Bette Maki, whose property at 0 Meadow Street in Carver, Massachusetts, was used for sand and gravel extraction. The mining operation had continued for more than a decade, with the couple raising concerns about its effects on their home and surrounding neighbourhood. According to the trial findings, the jury held both G. Lopes Construction and Maki liable for private nuisance, finding that their involvement in the operation substantially and unreasonably interfered with the couple's use and enjoyment of their property.Responsibility for this claim was divided, with 80% assigned to the construction company and 20% to the landowner.The verdict covered three legal claims: Nuisance, negligence and negligent trespass. Under the negligent-trespass claim, the jury awarded the couple $200,000 each for pain and suffering, along with $15,000 each for property damage. A further $100,000 was awarded under the negligence claim, bringing the total damages to $530,000. With mandatory interest, the amount is expected to exceed $760,000.The scale of the mining activity was a significant part of the case. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that the operation generated at least 54,000 truck trips over its 13-year run, with heavy vehicles passing within approximately 35 feet of the couple's front door. On some days, the number of trips reportedly reached 120. Residents described persistent noise, vibrations and dust accumulating on their cars, outdoor spaces and other parts of their properties.The trial also examined the potential health implications of the dust. Environmental engineering expert Scott Hersey presented laboratory findings identifying respirable crystalline silica in samples collected from the mining site. His analysis of more than a million weather observations found that winds had travelled from the mine towards the couple's home before 20 of 25 documented dust incidents.Pulmonary specialist Stephen L. Newman also testified about the residents' respiratory complaints and the possible effects of prolonged silica exposure. His assessment raised concerns about potential silica-related lung complications. However, neither resident received a confirmed diagnosis of silicosis, and the medical testimony should not be confused with a diagnosis delivered by the jury.The couple's legal battle had begun well before the trial. They had reportedly brought complaints about the mining activity to Carver town officials as early as 2014, raising concerns about dust, excessive truck traffic, noise and vibrations. Their lawsuit was filed in April 2023, challenging the operation and seeking relief over its impact on neighbouring properties. An attempt to secure an injunction to stop the excavation while the case was pending was rejected by a Superior Court judge in July 2023. The operation continued until March 2024, despite further objections from residents and legal proceedings surrounding the permits.The case has also drawn attention beyond Carver, where sand and gravel extraction has become a wider environmental and community concern. A separate report by the New Bedford Light in April 2026 examined how large-scale excavation in southeastern Massachusetts affects nearby residents, particularly through dust emissions and concerns about groundwater resources. The Plymouth Independent subsequently highlighted the Beadling verdict as an important development for communities dealing with similar mining disputes.The Meadow Street operation involved excavation across approximately 19 acres, with experts also examining its proximity to the Plymouth-Carver Sole Source Aquifer, an important regional drinking water resource. The case has brought renewed attention to the effects of commercial sand extraction on residential neighbourhoods and the responsibility of operators to prevent their activities from affecting neighbouring properties.
Article Summary: Josephine and Keith Beadling brought the case against G. Lopes Construction Inc. and landowner Bette Maki. Their property at 0 Meadow Street in Carver, Massachusetts, was used for sand and gravel extraction. The mining operation had continued for more than a decade, with the couple raising concerns about its effects on their home.

Article Title: Meet Donovan Atkinson, the 5-year-old who turned cucumbers from his family's garden into a pickle business and sold more than 500 jars from his roadside stand
Article Text:
PC: Facebook

How Donovan and his mother turned cucumbers into pickles

More than 500 jars sold under The Pickle Kid name

What running a pickle stand is teaching the five-year-old

The five-year-old has bigger plans for his pickle venture

A roadside stand selling homemade pickles is not the usual sight associated with a five-year-old. Yet Donovan Atkinson, a young boy from Attleboro, Massachusetts, has found himself running just such a venture, with cucumbers from his family's garden providing the starting point. What began with a surplus of home-grown vegetables eventually developed into a small business, complete with its own name, customers and jars carrying a distinctive label. Known locally as 'The Pickle Kid', Donovan has already sold more than 500 jars since setting up his stand in 2025. His experience has also introduced him to some of the everyday responsibilities involved in selling a product.The idea came about after Donovan's family grew more cucumbers than they could readily use in their garden. Rather than letting the extra produce go to waste, he and his mother, Gabrielle Atkinson, started experimenting with making pickles at home.The kitchen became the first place where the project took shape. Donovan worked alongside his mother, turning the garden harvest into jars of pickled cucumbers. For Donovan, the process offered a way to do something with the vegetables he had helped grow. It also gave the family an idea that could extend beyond their own kitchen.In 2025, Donovan took the next step and opened a roadside pickle stand. The small venture gave him an opportunity to sell the jars to people outside his immediate family and circle of friends.The response was enough to turn the project into a growing local activity. More than 500 jars have since been sold, with customers including neighbours, friends and people who happened to pass by the stand.His business became known as ‘The Pickle Kid’, a name that reflects both his age and the product he sells. The nickname has also become part of the presentation, appearing on the jars themselves.Selling the jars has given Donovan some early experience with the practical side of running a business. Each sale involves more than handing over a product. He has opportunities to count money, speak with customers and become familiar with the small interactions that come with selling something to the public.His mother has been involved throughout the process, helping him make the pickles and supporting the activity as it developed. At his age, the business remains a family-supported undertaking, but Donovan has already become familiar with several aspects of customer service and basic money management.The experience has also helped him build confidence when dealing with people who visit the stand. These are skills that extend beyond the immediate business, even as the pickle sales remain the main focus.The roadside stand is only the beginning of what Donovan would like to achieve. According to the WCVB report, he hopes to develop The Pickle Kid into a full pickle business in the future. For now, the operation remains centred on the small-scale sales that grew out of his family's garden. There is no indication that the business has moved into wider commercial production, but the more than 500 jars already sold give an idea of how far the original project has travelled. At five, he is still at the beginning of his entrepreneurial experience. But The Pickle Kid already has a name, a roadside stand and a growing customer base.
Article Summary: Donovan Atkinson and his mother grew more cucumbers than they could use in their garden. The five-year-old started experimenting with making pickles in the kitchen. In 2025, he opened a roadside pickle stand in Attleboro, Massachusetts. More than 500 jars have already been sold, with customers including neighbours, friends and people who happened to pass by.

Article Title: Watch: US Centcom shows strike commercial vessel in Hormuz that allegedly defied Iran blockade
Article Text:
Smoke rises from the stern of a St. Kitts-flagged cargo vessel following what US Central Command says was a strike on Saturday to disable the vessel, which was trying to break the US blockade of Iran, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman

Trump confirms fresh US strikes

Qatar pushes two-day bridge deal

Nuclear programme remains key sticking point

The US Central Command (Centcom) on Saturday released a video showing a commercial vessel being struck in what it described as the Gulf of Oman, after US forces disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship that allegedly ignored repeated warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. The disclosure came amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran and fresh efforts by mediators to revive negotiations to end the conflict.Centcom said the vessel was disabled after it failed to comply with multiple warnings. The US military has been enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports for months, including in waters around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments."CENTCOM forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 7, after the ship’s civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," it said.The latest disclosure comes nearly a month after the last confirmed US strike on a cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman.It also follows at least two reported instances in which Centcom did not publicly acknowledge military strikes in the region. Officials at the command had declined to confirm reports of explosions when questioned about them.Meanwhile, Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz and at the port of Jask on Saturday evening. The cause of the explosions was not immediately clear. The US military did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.Iran's military also said late Saturday that two tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the vessels' flags or destinations.The latest maritime incident comes days after US President Donald Trump confirmed that American forces had carried out fresh, limited strikes against Iran.Trump said on Friday that the US military had targeted an Iranian air defence system. Describing the action to reporters as “minor”, he confirmed the strikes. However, Centcom did not comment on the operation, even after Trump's remarks.For weeks, Trump had said he was considering a fresh wave of strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3. The possibility of a return to full-scale military operations has raised concerns across the Middle East and beyond. The US had not resumed such operations since the pause in fighting nearly two months ago.Even as military tensions persist, diplomatic efforts are continuing to find a way out of the conflict.Two Middle Eastern government officials said on Friday that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by Qatar, the chief mediator, to address differences with Washington over Tehran's nuclear programme.Regional officials said the proposal envisages a two-day arrangement involving confidence-building measures by both sides. On the first day, the US would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release some of the billions of dollars in Iranian assets frozen under sanctions.In return, Tehran would allow International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to access nuclear sites bombed by the US and Israel.On the second day, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a modified arrangement it has reached with Oman. The proposal has not yet received US approval. The arrangement would remain temporary until a permanent agreement on the waterway is reached with other Gulf countries.Once these measures are implemented, Washington and Tehran would begin broader negotiations on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium and other aspects of its nuclear programme, the officials said.However, one of the officials said Iran was currently unwilling to negotiate its nuclear activities until Washington agrees to several conditions that Tehran wants included in any ceasefire agreement.These include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen assets, compensation for war damage and an end to hostilities across the region, including Israeli military operations in Lebanon.The officials spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to comment publicly on the negotiations.Differences over Iran's nuclear programme remain the biggest obstacle to a broader agreement. Trump has insisted that the issue must be resolved as part of any deal to end the more than eight-month-old conflict.Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes. However, according to the IAEA, Tehran has 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% purity. This is a relatively short technical step away from the 90% enrichment level generally considered weapons-grade. There is no civilian energy application for uranium enriched to such high levels.The conflict began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran, seeking to destabilise its regime and destroy its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes.In June, Iran agreed to a memorandum of understanding with the US that outlined a path towards a permanent settlement. However, the understanding quickly unravelled as both sides accused each other of violating its terms.
Article Summary: US Central Command released a video showing a commercial vessel being struck in what it described as the Gulf of Oman. US forces disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship that allegedly ignored repeated warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. The US military has been enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports for months.

How the dispute over the house began

Why the trial court's decision was challenged

Why the husband retained credit for other expenses

Money earned or acquired before marriage may remain separate property, but putting it into a joint account can change its legal status. This became the central issue in a Florida divorce dispute involving a man who sold his Georgia home after marrying and used the proceeds, along with other funds, towards building a new house with his wife. When the marriage ended, he sought credit for the money he had originally contributed, arguing that it came from his separate property. However, the dispute took a different turn when the wife challenged the financial credits awarded to him by the trial court.In a November 4, 2026, opinion in Anderson v. Anderson, case number 2D2025-1747, the Florida Second District Court of Appeal ruled that the money used for the house's down payment had become marital property after being deposited into a joint bank account and used to finance a jointly titled home. The court reversed the portion of the divorce judgment that had awarded the husband credit for the down payment but upheld his right to receive credit for certain housing expenses he paid after separation. The ruling, available on Justia, sent the case back to the trial court for recalculation of the couple's financial settlement.The case involved Melyza C Anderson and Leland A Anderson, whose marriage lasted approximately two years.Before meeting Melyza, Leland owned a house in Georgia. After the couple married, they decided to relocate to Florida and build a home in Tampa.Leland sold his Georgia property and deposited the proceeds into a joint bank account held by the couple. He also transferred a lump sum of money he had earned through his employment into the same account. The couple used money from this account to make a down payment towards constructing their new house. The property was registered in both their names. Shortly after the house was completed, Melyza filed for divorce. Leland moved out but continued paying the monthly mortgage instalments and other expenses associated with the property for the next two years, leading up to the trial.Although Melyza continued living in the house, she did not contribute towards its mortgage payments or maintenance costs. During the divorce proceedings, Leland asked the court to give him financial credit for both the original down payment and the housing expenses he had paid after moving out.Melyza challenged both requests. She argued that the money from the Georgia property had become marital funds because Leland deposited it into their joint account and used it towards a home owned by both spouses. She also argued that his subsequent payments should be treated as temporary support rather than expenses for which he deserved reimbursement.The trial court granted Leland credit for the down payment as well as the housing expenses he had covered during the separation. Melyza appealed, arguing that the court had incorrectly treated the original contribution as his separate property. The appeals court examined Florida's rules governing marital and nonmarital assets. Under Florida law, property acquired separately by either spouse can remain nonmarital. However, separately owned assets can lose that status when they are mixed with marital funds.The court explained that money deposited into a joint bank account creates a rebuttable presumption that the depositing spouse intended to give the other spouse an undivided one-half interest in the funds. The spouse seeking to retain the money's separate status must overcome this presumption through clear and convincing evidence.In this case, Leland could not meet that requirement. The court noted that he had deposited the proceeds from his Georgia home into a joint account, mixed them with other funds and then used the money towards a property titled in both spouses' names. The evidence therefore supported treating the down payment as marital property rather than his separate contribution.The appeals court reached a different conclusion regarding the mortgage and maintenance payments Leland made after moving out. It noted that he had continued paying the home's expenses for two years while Melyza lived there without contributing financially. The trial court had found that Melyza had sufficient income to contribute towards the property's upkeep and had not proved a need for temporary support. The appeals court found that this conclusion was supported by the evidence.It also referred to earlier Florida decisions recognising that reimbursement for marital property-related expenses paid by one spouse during separation depends on the circumstances of each case. Consequently, the appeals court reversed the financial credit awarded for the down payment but upheld the credit for the expenses Leland had paid after separation. It remanded the case to the trial court to recalculate the couple's equitable distribution, affirming the divorce judgment in all other respects.The decision highlights how the handling of premarital money can affect property division during divorce. Even when funds originally come from a home owned by one spouse before marriage, transferring them into a joint account and using them for jointly titled property can change their legal character.

Article Title: Milwaukee Bucks star Myles Turner has joined a campaign promising 250 pet meals for every point he scores and 1,000 for each three-pointer, following a WNBA player's completed 319,750-meal contributio
Article Text:
Supporters can follow Turner’s scoring performances online and watch his points translate into pet meals throughout the season.

Basketball points turned to pet food

A personal link to animal welfare

Following a successful WNBA campaign

A basketball player’s on-court performance could soon translate into thousands of meals for pets of families in need. Milwaukee Bucks center Myles Turner has joined an animal welfare campaign linking NBA scoring to support for underserved pet owners across the US. With a new partnership with Humane World for Animals, every point Turner scores during the 2026-2027 regular season will help feed pets, showing how pro athletes can use their athletic platforms to solve problems beyond the game.Turner has signed on as an ambassador for Humane World for Animals’ More Than a Pet campaign, which highlights families that can’t afford to give their pets the care they need, states the report.Turner will be involved in the organization's Points for Pets program as part of the association. For every point scored during the upcoming NBA regular season, 250 meals will be donated to pets in underserved communities. Every 3-pointer will provide 1,000 meals, adds the online report.The campaign will include an online progress tracker on the More Than a Pet website, where supporters can track Turner’s scoring performances and the number of meals those performances translate into throughout the season, also adds the report.That is at a time when access to basic pet care is still a big problem in the United States. According to Humane World for Animals, about 20 million pets live with families living in poverty, and of those animals, around 70 percent have never been to a vet.Turner’s involvement comes from his own history as a pet owner. In August 2018, his fiancée, Aysia McCloud, adopted their cat Casper from Operation Kindness, an animal shelter in Dallas. The eight-year-old domestic shorthair has since become a fixture in their home.Casper is a lovely boy who is affectionate and sociable. He likes to spend time with the family, have his daily brushing sessions and find sunny spots around the house. His love of squeezing himself into boxes of all shapes and sizes has also become a part of his unique personality.Eventually, the couple’s experience with Casper led to the creation of The Casper Foundation in December 2025. The animal welfare nonprofit primarily works with cats, partnering with shelters, helping with adoption efforts, and creating ways for people to get involved in animal welfare.Turner joins the campaign after a successful previous edition featuring Minnesota Lynx guard Kayla McBride in 2026. She scored 775 points including 126 three-pointers, contributing a total of 319,750 pet meals. Humane World for Animals reported that these meals were then donated and delivered to families across the country.The program kicked off in 2024 with Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball, who scored 1,184 points, which equated to 296,000 meals for pets.Turner’s participation will expose the program to a fresh NBA audience, extending its reach through one of the game’s premier defensive players.Support for families and their petsThe More Than a Pet campaign additionally emphasizes the need to keep pets with the families that love them, rather than letting financial troubles lead owners to give up their companions.Rural Area Veterinary Services, Pets for Life and other programs . Humane World for Animals supports this goal. In total, these programs have assisted more than 750,000 pets in underserved communities. That work involves distributing 38 million pounds of pet food and 12,800 pallets of pet supplies worth more than $130 million.With Turner’s participation, we will raise awareness about the need for accessible pet food, veterinary services and critical resources. This initiative shows how a basketball season can make a difference for a cause bigger than the scoreboard, with every basket an opportunity to help animals and the people who love them.Images Courtesy: istock and Instagram/mylesturner
Article Summary: Milwaukee Bucks center Myles Turner has joined an animal welfare campaign linking NBA scoring to support for underserved pet owners across the US. With a new partnership with Humane World for Animals, every point Turner scores during the 2026-2027 regular season will help feed pets. Supporters can follow Turner’s scoring performances online and watch his points translate into pet meals throughout the season.

Article Title: Michigan evaluated centerline rumble strips across nearly 5,400 miles of rural roads; target crashes fell 47%, and target fatal crashes fell 51%
Article Text:
AI representation of road workers installing and inspecting centerline rumble strips on a rural two-lane highway, a safety measure designed to alert drivers when their vehicles drift across the centerline. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

How centerline rumble strips work

What the Michigan evaluation found

To boost road safety, the Michigan Department of Transportation has installed centerline rumble strips on rural roads, resulting in a 47% decrease in target crashes and a 51% decrease in fatalities. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Research supports the wider use of rumble strips

One simple application of roadside safety innovations yielded strong outcomes across nearly 5,400 miles of rural roads in Michigan. Centerline rumble strips reduced target crashes by 47% and fatal crashes by 51%. The initiative, led by the Michigan Department of Transportation , emphasises control to avoid vehicles crossing the centerline into the traffic lane. The study compared crash data from the three years before and the three years after the improvements. The findings emphasised that modest improvements in road surfacing, which are relatively low cost, can make a difference for some of the worst crashes occurring on rural high-speed roads.Centreline rumble strips are small, shallow grooves that are cut into the pavement surface along the road centreline, generally under or near the centreline markings. Tires rolling across the grooves vibrate and rattle, and this sound and vibration notify drivers that their vehicle may be leaving the lane.The warning is most effective when the driver becomes distracted or tired and loses concentration for a time. Instead of having to spot the marking on the road themselves, the grooves act as a physical reminder for the driver to realign the steering before moving into the oncoming traffic lane.Rumble strips can be installed on existing roads as a post-construction road engineering measure, and they are seen as a relatively inexpensive option for roads where opposing traffic flows are not physically separated.MDOT initiated and completed the state-wide centerline rumble strip installation project between 2008 and 2010. The department installed the strips on rural non-freeway highways with a posted speed limit of 55 miles per hour. The project was 54 miles long, and shoulder rumble strips were also installed along some of the wider shoulders.The study considered 3 crash types: head-on crashes, side-swipe crashes between vehicles moving in opposite directions, and single-vehicle crashes where the driver departs the road to the left. The data reveal 2,488 target crashes for the before period and 1,306 in the after period. The study revealed a statistically significant reduction in all three types of crashes and a 51% decrease in fatalities within the target group.The researchers controlled for snowfall variation by excluding crashes in which snowy or icy pavement was noted as a contributing factor, reducing the chance that winter weather would distort the comparison. The researchers also show the programme's worth. Their benefit-cost ratio, ranging from 18:1 to 58:1 depending on the discount rate applied in the analysis, showed potential financial gain from preventing severe crashes far exceeded installation costs.Michigan's findings are consistent with research conducted in other parts of the United States. A study published in Accident Analysis & Prevention in 2025 examined centreline rumble strips on rural two-lane roads in Maine. It found reductions of between 28% and 48% in head-on, opposite-direction side-Y collisions, with an estimated benefit at least 14 times the installation cost. Another study published in the Journal of Transportation Engineering in 2016 examined the effectiveness of centreline and shoulder rumble strips on rural roads in Kentucky, Missouri, and Pennsylvania. Overall, the report detected A 36.8% reduction in head-on crashes, but the combined reduction in lane-departure crashes was a test assessed to be in the order of 27%Findings from the studies suggest that Rumble strips can provide quantifiable safety benefits for various types of road systems, but rumble strips do not work equally well on all roads, with the design of installation and the type of crashes targeted as factors. The program also showed how safety can integrate into the day-to-day work of road maintenance, and Michigan MDOT is transitioning to a contract for annual payment, marking a more efficient installation process and eliminating the need for dedicated construction projects.
Article Summary: Centerline rumble strips are small, shallow grooves that are cut into the pavement surface along the road centreline. Tires rolling across the grooves vibrate and rattle, and this sound and vibration notify drivers that their vehicle may be leaving the lane. The warning is most effective when the driver becomes distracted or tired and loses concentration for a time.

Article Title: Chained to bed, windows covered in foil: How ex-husband held US woman captive for 2 years
Article Text:
40-year-old Arturo Calzada-Becerril and his girlfriend, Erendira Amoles, 41, pose in a police photo following their arrest on kidnapping and assault charges​

Woman allegedly brought from Mexico and held captive

Two accused face kidnapping charges

Neighbours shocked by discovery

A woman in Fargo, North Dakota, was rescued after allegedly being chained to a bed for two years, beaten and sexually assaulted by her ex-husband and his girlfriend, police said. The woman was found after a maintenance worker heard her cries for help at an apartment complex on November 3.Officers responding to the building found her restrained by a heavy chain and padlock around her right ankle, with the chain secured to the bedframe, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.A maintenance technician had reported hearing muffled screams from the apartment, prompting the building management to call 911.The victim was taken to hospital after being freed. Police interviewed her with the help of a translator, as she communicated through a translation app, according to the reports.Her ex-husband, 40-year-old Arturo Calzada-Becerril, and his girlfriend, 41-year-old Erendira Amoles, have been charged in connection with the case.According to court documents cited by Valley News Live, the woman told investigators that Calzada-Becerril brought her to Fargo from Mexico in 2024 and kept her confined in the apartment, where she was not allowed to leave.The bedroom reportedly had a security camera pointed towards the bed, while its windows were covered with aluminium foil.The woman said she was given food twice a day and forced to use a bucket beside the bed as a toilet.Investigators found bruising on her arms, legs and face. She also told police that Calzada-Becerril and Amoles had beaten and sexually assaulted her. She said she had been punched, leaving a scar on her forehead.An investigative report cited by Inforum described the restraints as chains secured to the bed's headboard and footboard with large bolts, washers and nuts. The chains were covered with foam pool noodles and secured with Master Lock padlocks.Court documents state that Calzada-Becerril told police he kept the woman restrained so that "she did not run away", claiming she was addicted to drugs and that he did not want her to start using again.Prosecutors alleged that the pair held the woman captive to obtain immigration status.
